newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Sabena says Swissair may pull out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sabena says Swissair may pull out.

text.p: The head of the Belgian airline Sabena said on Thursday that Swiss Air was effectively threatening to abandon its 49.5 stake in the partly state-owned airline unless loss-making Sabena starts making profits.
Sabena chief executive Paul Reutlinger said that Swissair was considering a writeoff of its investment in the Belgian airline.

"The threat is to write off the investment, but what it means is to have the liberty to take any decision afterwards. (This) includes Swissair walking away," Reutlinger told Reuters after a news conference.
Swissair might write off its investment if the return was insufficient, Reutlinger said.
Swissair, which took over the running of Sabena in 1995, said at the time it would invest six billion Belgian francs ($193 million) as part of a 10 billion franc capital injection plan.
"If Swissair cannot hope to find a return on investment in Sabena...everyone in charge would decide not to invest any more and pull out of that company," said Reutlinger, a Swissair appointee.
He said Swissair was seeking a return on capital employed of four percent in 1998, six percent in 1999, eight percent in 2000 and 10 to 12 percent thereafter.
"You always have to take into account that the investor (Swissair) has several options. If we want to keep the investor with us, we have to get at a return of 10 to 12 percent," Reutlinger said.

A Swissair spokesman in Zurich said it would not make a decision on whether to write-off its Sabena stake before the end of this year. He added that Swissair currently had no plans to pull out of the Belgian carrier.
Reutlinger made his remarks after announcing a draft deal with four Belgian trade union on a 4.7 billion Belgian francs ($151 million) recovery plan for Sabena.

But he said there was also "bad news", as Sabena pilots had gone on strike to protest against the plan. A Sabena spokesman said 25 of the 70 flights so far on Thursday had been cancelled. The Sabena group has 175 flights per day.
The "Horizon 98' plan includes job cuts, adjustments in flexibility and working conditions and a two-year wage freeze.
Reutlinger said members of the pilots' association within the trade unions had pulled out of the negotiations two days ago but he was still hopeful of convincing them to accept the deal.
"I will return to the pilots association to tell them that the future of Sabena is now at stake," he said.
"I'm determined to stick to the agreement with the unions, I have no intention of going back on it," said Reutlinger.
Reutlinger said he thought the pilots had withdrawn because they did not feel properly represented by the unions.

Sabena had a 1995 group loss before provisions of 530 million francs compared with a 1.23 billion francs loss in 1994. Reutlinger said earlier this year that earnings had been lagging company expectations due to the strikes.
"Results are not good. We are still suffering from the strikes in February, we still don't have all our clients back," he said.
Swissair has blamed Sabena for a large part of a 27 million Swiss franc ($21.5 million) first-half loss at Swissair's associated companies.
